title: Book II: Old And Young — Chapter XXII
paragraphs:
“We talked for a long time; she was simple and kind.
Knowing nothing of evil, she did good;
From the riches of her heart she gave me charity,
And as I listened, as a heart gives itself,
I gave her mine without daring to think of it.
She carried my life away and never knew.”
—ALFRED DE MUSSET.

At dinner the following day, Will Ladislaw was delightful company and gave Mr. Casaubon no occasion to disapprove. On the contrary, Dorothea thought she had never seen anyone draw her husband into conversation so successfully or listen to him with such respectful attention. Admittedly, the listeners around Tipton were not especially gifted. Will spoke a good deal himself, but his comments came so quickly and with such an air of incidental unimportance that they seemed a cheerful little chime following a great bell. Whatever his failings at other times, this was certainly one of his good days. He described small incidents among Rome's poor that only someone free to roam could have witnessed. He agreed with Mr. Casaubon about Middleton's unsound opinions on the relationship between Judaism and Catholicism. Then he moved easily into an account, half enthusiastic and half playful, of his pleasure in Rome's very mixture of things. Constant comparison made the mind flexible and prevented one from seeing the world's successive ages as separate boxes with no living connection. Mr. Casaubon's studies, Will remarked, had always been too broad for that, so perhaps he had never experienced such a sudden change. For himself, though, Rome had given him a wholly new sense of history as a whole. Its fragments stirred his imagination and made him build connections. From time to time, though not too often, he appealed to Dorothea and discussed her replies as though her feelings deserved a place in the final judgment even of the Madonna di Foligno or the Laocoön. Feeling that one helps form the world's opinion makes conversation especially cheerful. Mr. Casaubon, too, took some pride in his young wife, who spoke better than most women, as he had recognized when choosing her.

Everything was going so pleasantly that, when Mr. Casaubon said his work in the Library would pause for two days and, after one brief return, leave him no further reason to stay in Rome, Will ventured to urge a visit to a studio or two before Mrs. Casaubon left. Wouldn't Mr. Casaubon take her? It was something not to be missed, something distinctive: a form of life growing like fresh little vegetation, with its population of insects, on enormous fossils. Will would gladly guide them, not through anything tiring, just a few examples.

Seeing Dorothea look earnestly towards him, Mr. Casaubon could hardly avoid asking whether such visits would interest her. He was at her service for the entire day now. They agreed that Will would return the next morning and drive with them.

Will could not leave out Thorwaldsen, a living celebrity about whom even Mr. Casaubon asked. But before much of the day had passed, he led them to his friend Adolf Naumann's studio. He described Naumann as a leading renewer of Christian art, one of those who had not merely revived but enlarged the grand conception of supreme events as sacred mysteries watched by successive ages, bringing the great souls of all periods into a kind of shared present. Will added that for the time being he had made himself Naumann's pupil.

“I've been doing some oil sketches under his guidance,” Will said. “I hate copying. I must add something of my own. Naumann has been painting the Saints Drawing the Chariot of the Church, and I've been sketching Marlowe's Tamburlaine Driving the Conquered Kings in His Chariot. I'm less ecclesiastical than Naumann, and sometimes tease him about cramming in too much meaning. But this time I intend to surpass him in the breadth of my purpose. To me, Tamburlaine in his chariot represents the tremendous course of the world's physical history, whipping the harnessed dynasties onward. I think that's a good mythical interpretation.” He looked at Mr. Casaubon, who received this casual handling of symbolism very uneasily and gave a noncommittal bow.
“It must be a very grand sketch to convey so much,” said Dorothea. “I'd need an explanation even of your explanation. Is Tamburlaine meant to represent earthquakes and volcanoes?”
“Oh yes,” Will said, laughing, “and the migrations of peoples, the clearing of forests, America, and the steam engine. Anything you can imagine!”
“What difficult shorthand!” said Dorothea, smiling at her husband. “It would take all your knowledge to read it.”
Mr. Casaubon blinked furtively at Will, suspecting he was being mocked. But he could not include Dorothea in that suspicion.

They found Naumann hard at work, though without a model. His pictures were arranged to advantage, and a dove-gray smock and maroon velvet cap set off his plain but lively appearance. Everything was as fortunate as though he had expected the beautiful young Englishwoman at precisely that moment.

In confident English the painter gave short explanations of his finished and unfinished subjects, apparently observing Mr. Casaubon as closely as Dorothea. Will broke in now and then with enthusiastic praise, pointing out particular strengths in his friend's work. Dorothea began to gain entirely new ideas about Madonnas seated beneath inexplicable canopied thrones against simple countryside, and saints holding models of buildings or with knives seemingly lodged by accident in their skulls. Things that had appeared monstrous were becoming understandable, even natural in meaning. But this was evidently a field of knowledge Mr. Casaubon had never cared to explore.
“I think I'd rather feel a painting's beauty than have to solve it like a riddle,” Dorothea told Will. “Still, I could learn to understand these pictures sooner than yours with its enormous meaning.”
“Don't mention my painting in front of Naumann,” said Will. “He'll tell you it's all botchwork. That's his strongest insult!”
“Is that true?” Dorothea asked, turning her honest eyes towards Naumann. He made a slight face and answered:
“Oh, he isn't serious about painting. Literature must be his field. That is wi-ide.”

The way Naumann stretched the vowel made the word sound satirical. Will rather disliked it, but managed a laugh. Mr. Casaubon, though somewhat repelled by the painter's German accent, began to respect his discriminating severity.
That respect did not lessen when Naumann drew Will aside briefly, glanced from a large canvas to Mr. Casaubon, then approached again and said:

“My friend Ladislaw thinks you will forgive me, sir, if I say that a sketch of your head would be invaluable for the St. Thomas Aquinas in that picture. It's too much to ask, but I so rarely see exactly what I need: the ideal embodied in reality.”

“You astonish me, sir,” said Mr. Casaubon, a glow of pleasure improving his appearance. “But if my poor features, which I have always considered entirely ordinary, could supply any traits for the Angelic Doctor, I would feel honored. Provided, that is, that the process is not lengthy and Mrs. Casaubon does not object to waiting.”
Nothing could have pleased Dorothea more, unless a miraculous voice had declared Mr. Casaubon the wisest and worthiest of men. Then her wavering faith would have become firm again.

Naumann's equipment was astonishingly ready, and both sketching and conversation began at once. Dorothea sat down in peaceful silence, happier than she had been for a long time. Everyone around her seemed good. She told herself that, had she only been less ignorant, Rome would have been full of beauty; its sadness would have taken flight on wings of hope. No one was less suspicious by nature. As a child she had believed wasps could feel gratitude and sparrows respond to honor, and her indignation had matched her faith when their baseness became clear.
The skillful painter asked Mr. Casaubon about English political institutions, drawing lengthy replies. Meanwhile Will perched on a set of steps at the back, overlooking the scene.
Presently Naumann said, “Now, if I could set this aside for half an hour and return to it—come and look, Ladislaw—I think it's perfect so far.”
Will uttered those emphatic exclamations which suggest admiration too strong for grammar. Naumann then said with pitiable regret:
“Ah, if only I could have a little longer. But you have other engagements. I couldn't ask it, or even ask you to return tomorrow.”
“Oh, let's stay!” said Dorothea. “We have nothing planned today except going about, do we?” She looked pleadingly at Mr. Casaubon. “It would be a pity not to make the head as good as possible.”
“I am at your service, sir,” said Mr. Casaubon with gracious condescension. “Since I have surrendered the inside of my head to idleness, its outside may as well work in this fashion.”

“You are extraordinarily kind. Now I'm happy!” said Naumann. He continued in German to Will, pointing at different places in the sketch as though discussing it. Setting it aside, he looked vaguely around, apparently seeking something to occupy his guests. Then he turned to Mr. Casaubon.
“Perhaps the beautiful bride, the gracious lady, would allow me to fill the interval by attempting a small sketch of her. Not for that picture, of course, as you see. Just a separate study.”
Bowing, Mr. Casaubon said he was sure Mrs. Casaubon would oblige. Dorothea immediately asked, “Where should I stand?”

Naumann apologized repeatedly as he asked her to stand and allowed himself to arrange her pose. She complied without the artificial gestures and laughter often thought necessary on such occasions. “I want you as Santa Clara,” he said. “Leaning like this, your cheek against your hand. Like that. Please look at that stool. There!”
Will was torn between wanting to fall at the saint's feet and kiss her robe, and wanting to knock Naumann down as he adjusted her arm. It was all insolence and desecration. He regretted bringing her.

The painter worked diligently. Recovering himself, Will moved about and entertained Mr. Casaubon as ingeniously as possible. In the end, however, he could not prevent the gentleman from finding the time long; Mr. Casaubon made this clear by worrying that his wife would become tired. Naumann understood the hint.
“Now, sir, if you would oblige me again, I can release your lady wife.”

Mr. Casaubon's patience endured a little longer. When it finally appeared that St. Thomas Aquinas's head would benefit from another sitting, he agreed to return the next day. Santa Clara, too, received more than one touch-up on that visit. Mr. Casaubon was so far from displeased with the result that he arranged to buy the picture in which St. Thomas Aquinas sat among the Church's learned doctors in a debate too abstract to depict, attended with varying degrees of interest by an audience overhead. When the Santa Clara was mentioned afterwards, Naumann declared himself dissatisfied. He could not conscientiously promise to make a worthy picture of it. The arrangement concerning Santa Clara therefore remained conditional.

I will not linger over Naumann's jokes about Mr. Casaubon that evening, or his ecstatic praises of Dorothea's charm. Will joined in both, but with a difference. As soon as Naumann named any detail of her beauty, Will grew angry at his presumption. Even his most ordinary words seemed coarse. What business had he discussing her lips? She was not a woman to be spoken of like other women. Will could not say exactly what he meant, but he became irritable. Yet when, after some resistance, he had agreed to bring the Casaubons to the studio, he had been tempted by the pride of being able to grant Naumann a chance to study her loveliness—or rather, her divinity, since phrases applicable to mere physical prettiness could not apply to her. Certainly everyone in Tipton and the surrounding area, as well as Dorothea herself, would have been surprised at such attention to her beauty. There, Miss Brooke had merely been a “fine young woman.”
“Do me a favor and drop the subject, Naumann. Mrs. Casaubon isn't to be discussed as though she were a model,” said Will. Naumann stared.

“Very well! I'll discuss my Aquinas. Not a bad type of head, after all. I suspect the great scholar himself would have been flattered by a request for his portrait. Nobody equals these stiff scholars for vanity! Just as I expected, he cared much less about her portrait than his own.”

“He's a damned bloodless, pedantic fool,” Will burst out through clenched teeth. Naumann knew nothing of his debt to Mr. Casaubon, but Will was thinking of it himself and wishing a check could settle it all.
Naumann shrugged. “A good thing they're leaving soon, my dear fellow. They're ruining your pleasant temper.”

All Will's hopes and schemes now centered on seeing Dorothea alone. He wanted only to make a stronger impression, to occupy a more special place in her memory than he could yet expect. Her open, eager goodwill, which he recognized as her usual disposition, made him rather impatient. Worshiping a woman enthroned beyond reach plays a large part in men's lives. Yet most worshipers long for some royal acknowledgment, some approving gesture with which their soul's sovereign can encourage them without descending from her throne. That was precisely what Will wanted. But his imagination made contradictory demands. It was beautiful to see Dorothea's eyes turn towards Mr. Casaubon with wifely anxiety and entreaty. Without that dutiful concern, she would have lost some of her halo. The next moment, however, her husband's absorption of such nectar, like water sinking into sand, became unbearable. Will's longing to say damaging things about him was perhaps all the more tormenting because he had such strong reasons to restrain it.
Will had no invitation to dinner the following day. He therefore persuaded himself that he ought to call, and that the only suitable time was midday, when Mr. Casaubon would be out.

Dorothea did not know that her earlier reception of Will had displeased her husband. She had no hesitation in receiving him, especially as he might have come to say goodbye. When he entered, she was examining cameos she had bought for Celia. She welcomed him as though his visit were perfectly natural and, holding a cameo bracelet, immediately said:

“I'm so glad you've come. Perhaps you know about cameos and can tell me whether these are really good. I wanted you with us when we chose them, but Mr. Casaubon thought there wasn't time. He finishes his work tomorrow, and we leave in three days. I've been worried about the cameos. Please sit down and examine them.”
“I'm no expert, but you can't go far wrong with these little scenes from Homer. They're exquisitely carved. And the color is lovely. It will suit you perfectly.”

“Oh, they're for my sister, whose coloring is quite different. You saw her with me at Lowick. She's fair-haired and very pretty, at least I think so. We've never been apart so long before. She's a darling and has never done anything wrong in her life. Before leaving, I discovered she wanted me to buy her some cameos. I'd be sorry if they weren't good examples of their kind.” Dorothea smiled as she added the last qualification.
“You don't seem very fond of cameos,” said Will, sitting some distance away and watching her close the cases.
“No. Frankly, I don't consider them a great purpose in life,” said Dorothea.
“I'm afraid you're a heretic about art in general. Why? I would have expected you to respond strongly to beauty everywhere.”

“I suppose I'm slow to understand many things,” Dorothea said simply. “I'd like to make life beautiful—everyone's life, I mean. And all this enormous expenditure on art, which somehow seems to stand outside life and do nothing to improve it for the world, is painful. My pleasure in anything is spoiled when I'm reminded that most people are shut out of it.”

“That's sympathy turned fanatical,” Will said impulsively. “You could say the same about landscape, poetry, every refinement. Follow the idea through, and you ought to be miserable about your own goodness and turn wicked to avoid having an advantage over others. The best piety is enjoyment, when you can manage it. That's how you do most to preserve the earth's reputation as an agreeable planet. Enjoyment spreads. Trying to take care of the whole world is useless. You're already helping it when you take delight in art or anything else. Would you turn all the world's young people into a tragic chorus, wailing and moralizing over misery? I suspect you mistakenly believe suffering is virtuous and want to make your life a martyrdom.” He had gone further than intended and stopped himself. Dorothea's thoughts, however, were not following the same course. She answered without particular emotion:

“You really misunderstand me. I'm not a sad, melancholy person. I never stay unhappy for long. I'm angry and naughty, unlike Celia. I have a great outburst, and then everything seems glorious again. I can't help believing blindly in glorious things. I'd gladly enjoy the art here, but there's so much I don't understand, so much that seems to make ugliness sacred instead of beauty. The painting and sculpture may be wonderful, but the feeling is often low and brutal, sometimes even ridiculous. Here and there something strikes me immediately as noble, something I could compare to the Alban Mountains or sunset from the Pincian Hill. That only makes it more regrettable that so little of the best kind exists among all these things men have labored over.”
“Of course there's always plenty of poor work. The rare things need that soil to grow in.”

“Oh dear,” said Dorothea, drawing that thought into the main current of her anxiety. “I can see how difficult it must be to do anything good. Since coming to Rome, I've often thought that most of our lives would look uglier and more clumsy than the pictures if they could be hung on a wall.”
She opened her lips as though to continue, then changed her mind and stopped.

“You're too young for those thoughts. They're out of place at your age,” Will said forcefully, with his habitual quick shake of the head. “You speak as if you'd never had any youth. It's monstrous, as though you'd seen Hades in childhood, like the boy in the legend. You've been raised among those dreadful ideas that choose the sweetest women to devour, like Minotaurs. And now you'll be shut up in that stone prison at Lowick, buried alive. The thought makes me furious. I'd rather never have met you than imagine such a future for you.”

Again Will feared he had gone too far. But the meaning we give words depends on our feelings. His angry regret carried so much kindness for Dorothea's heart, which had always poured out warmth and received so little from those around her, that she felt a new gratitude. With a gentle smile she answered:
“It's very kind of you to worry about me. It's because you disliked Lowick yourself. You had your heart set on a different life. But Lowick is the home I've chosen.”

The last words came with an almost solemn rhythm. Will did not know what to say. Kneeling to embrace her slippers and declaring he would die for her would be useless; plainly she required nothing of the sort. They were silent briefly. Then Dorothea began again, as though finally approaching what had been in her thoughts all along.

“I wanted to ask about something you said the other day. Perhaps it was partly your lively way of speaking. I've noticed you like putting things strongly. I often exaggerate myself when I speak hastily.”
“What was it?” asked Will, noticing an unfamiliar hesitation in her voice. “My tongue is given to exaggeration. It catches fire as it goes. I expect I'll have to take it back.”

“What you said about the need to know German, for the subjects Mr. Casaubon studies. I've been thinking about it. With his learning, surely he must have the same materials available as the German scholars?” Her hesitation came from a dim awareness of the strange position she occupied: consulting someone else about the adequacy of her husband's scholarship.

“Not exactly the same materials,” said Will, intending to be properly restrained. “He isn't a specialist in Eastern languages and cultures, you know. He doesn't claim more than secondhand knowledge there.”

“But there are valuable books on antiquity written long ago by scholars who knew nothing of these modern developments, and people still use them. Why shouldn't Mr. Casaubon's work be valuable too?” Dorothea asked, with greater energy in her protest. She felt compelled to argue aloud the case she had been arguing in her mind.

“That depends on the field,” Will replied, his tone also becoming argumentative. “Mr. Casaubon's subject changes as much as chemistry. New discoveries keep creating new perspectives. Who wants a system based on the four elements, or a book refuting Paracelsus? Don't you see that there's no point now in crawling a little way behind last century's men, people like Bryant, and correcting their mistakes? Living in a storeroom of junk, polishing broken-legged theories about Chus and Mizraim?”

“How can you speak so lightly?” Dorothea asked, looking both sorrowful and angry. “If you're right, what could be sadder than so much devoted work wasted? I'm surprised it doesn't hurt you more, if you really believe a man as good, able, and learned as Mr. Casaubon might fail in the work of his best years.” She was beginning to feel shocked that she had allowed even this possibility and angry with Will for leading her to it.

“You asked me about facts, not feelings,” said Will. “But if you want to punish me for the facts, I submit. I'm in no position to express my feelings about Mr. Casaubon. At best it would sound like praise from someone he supports.”

“Please forgive me,” Dorothea said, blushing deeply. “As you say, it was my fault for raising the subject. Indeed, I'm entirely wrong. Failing after long perseverance is much nobler than never making an effort worthy of the name of failure.”

“I agree completely,” Will said, determined to change the situation. “So completely that I've decided not to risk never achieving even a failure. Mr. Casaubon's generosity may have been dangerous for me. I mean to give up the freedom it has allowed. I'll return to England soon and make my own way, relying on nobody but myself.”
“That's admirable. I respect the feeling,” said Dorothea, her warmth returning. “But I'm certain Mr. Casaubon has never considered anything in the matter except your best interests.”
“Now she's married him, she has enough stubbornness and pride to take the place of love,” Will thought. Getting up, he said aloud:
“I won't see you again.”
“Oh, stay until Mr. Casaubon returns,” said Dorothea earnestly. “I'm so glad we met in Rome. I wanted to know you.”
“And I've made you angry,” said Will. “I've made you think badly of me.”

“Oh no. My sister says I'm always angry with people who don't say exactly what I want. But I hope I don't usually think badly of them. Afterwards I'm generally forced to think badly of myself for being impatient.”
“Still, you don't like me. I've made the thought of me unpleasant to you.”
“Not at all,” Dorothea said with completely open kindness. “I like you very much.”
Will was not entirely satisfied. Apparently he might have mattered more if she disliked him. He said nothing, but looked dejected, if not sulky.

“And I'm very interested to see what you do,” Dorothea continued brightly. “I firmly believe people have different natural callings. Without that belief I suppose I'd be very narrow-minded. There are so many things besides painting that I know nothing about. You'd hardly believe how little I've absorbed of music and literature, which you know so well. I wonder what your calling will prove to be. Perhaps a poet?”

“That depends. Being a poet means having a soul so quick to perceive that no shade of quality escapes it, and so quick to feel that perception becomes a hand playing delicately varied music on the strings of emotion. Knowledge turns instantly into feeling, and feeling flashes back as a new instrument of knowledge. A person may reach that state only at moments.”

“But you've left out the poems,” said Dorothea. “I think they're needed to complete a poet. I understand what you mean about knowledge turning into feeling, because that's just what seems to happen to me. But I'm certain I could never write a poem.”

“You ARE a poem. That's the best part of being a poet: what fills the poet's awareness in the finest moments,” said Will, displaying the originality we all share with morning, spring, and other endlessly recurring renewals.
“I'm very glad to hear it,” said Dorothea, her words lilting through laughter like birdsong, her eyes showing playful gratitude. “You say such kind things to me!”
“I wish I could ever do something you'd call kind, ever be of the smallest service to you. I'm afraid I'll never have the chance.” Will spoke passionately.

“Oh yes,” Dorothea said warmly. “The chance will come, and I'll remember your good wishes. I hoped from the first that we would be friends, because you're related to Mr. Casaubon.” A watery brightness filled her eyes, and Will felt his own filling too in obedience to a law of nature. Mentioning Mr. Casaubon would have spoiled everything if anything could then have broken the softening power and sweet dignity of her noble, unsuspecting inexperience.

“And there is something you can do even now,” said Dorothea. A returning impulse made her rise and walk a few steps. “Promise never to speak to anyone about that subject again, about Mr. Casaubon's writings, I mean, in that way. I led you into it. It was my fault. But promise me.”
She came back from her brief walk and stood facing Will, looking at him seriously.

“Certainly. I promise,” said Will, though he reddened. If he never said another cutting word about Mr. Casaubon and stopped accepting his favors, it would plainly be permissible to hate him all the more. A poet must know how to hate, Goethe says, and Will at least possessed that accomplishment. He said he must leave without waiting for Mr. Casaubon, but would call to say goodbye at the last opportunity. Dorothea held out her hand, and they exchanged a simple farewell.

Going out through the carriage entrance, however, he met Mr. Casaubon. After expressing good wishes for his cousin, that gentleman politely declined the pleasure of another farewell visit the next day, which would already be crowded with preparations for departure.

“There's something about our cousin Mr. Ladislaw I think will improve your opinion of him,” Dorothea told her husband that evening. As soon as he had come in, she had mentioned Will's visit and his intention to return. Mr. Casaubon had replied, “I met him outside, and I believe we said our final goodbyes,” with the manner and tone used to indicate that a subject, private or public, holds too little interest to invite another remark. Dorothea had therefore waited.
“What is it, my love?” asked Mr. Casaubon. He always said “my love” when his manner was coldest.

“He's decided to stop wandering immediately and no longer depend on your generosity. He means to return to England soon and earn his own way. I thought you'd see that as a good sign,” said Dorothea, looking pleadingly into her husband's expressionless face.
“Did he specify the precise occupation to which he intends to devote himself?”
“No. But he said he recognized the danger your generosity held for him. He'll write to you about it, of course. Don't you think better of him for deciding?”
“I shall wait for his letter on the subject,” said Mr. Casaubon.

“I told him I was certain you had considered only his welfare in everything you'd done. I remembered how kindly you spoke of him when I first saw him at Lowick,” Dorothea said, placing her hand on her husband's.

“I had a duty towards him,” said Mr. Casaubon, laying his other hand over hers in conscientious acceptance of her caress. He could not prevent an uneasy look. “Otherwise, I confess, the young man is of no particular interest to me. Nor need we discuss his future, which is not ours to determine beyond the limits I have sufficiently explained.” Dorothea did not speak of Will again.
